entries.title: Parametric Point Cloud Blend Space
entries.body:
# | PPCBS | A 3-Dimensional Blend-Space |

How many nice words can we fit in, to make it sound spacey?
Alot!

### PPCBS is a 3-Dimensional Blend-Space allowing Technical Animators to create complex locomotion systems, which purpose to facilitate creation of states such as Swimming, Flying but also Grounded Locomotion which provides additional input to allow sampling data such as Slopes or Stances.


#### Providing multiple blend algorithm's to support and cover varying use-cases, instead of guessing or hard-coding these, allowing designers to create complex and visually stunning Gameplay Animation Logic that fits their needs unrestricted and easy to implement.

##### These could be Omni-Directional Movement Spaces, provided the sampled space is correctly lined up. Non Planar Movement Behaviors and many more.

### Synchronizing Animations making sure their cyclic phase matches, which is useful in Grounded, but also Swimming scenarios, to avoid muddy transitions, sliding feet and bunny hopping.



## Runtime and Editor Showcase.

src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YPJ0_ISq-yg"

stay tuned and have a NICE DAY :) .

entries.title: Profiling Anim Graphs!
entries.body:
Profiling Animation Graphs can sometimes be tricky, especially in large systems where evaluation or code execution depends on nodes existing throughout the Anim Graph and maintaining valid node references.

In simpler cases, it’s possible to override certain graph evaluations using **pose caching**. 
This can work well, but only if dependencies like the ones mentioned above don’t prevent proper graph evaluation. Even then, the process can become tedious.

We can get a general overview of which systems affect performance using `stat anim` or Unreal Insights tracing. However, this still leaves a lot of room for guesswork, it works, but it can only hint.

To speed up this process, I created two custom nodes that allow me to evaluate the cost of specific sections throughout the Anim Graph without having to unplug layers or disconnect nodes.

![[Pasted image 20260301180014.png]]

These nodes automatically create a **stat scope cycle counter** based on their assigned section name.

We can place multiple instances of them throughout the Anim Graph to evaluate which sections are the most expensive, especially when optimization becomes necessary.

This would look as follows:
![[Pasted image 20260301180607.png]]

Using `Stat PATK_Profiling 1`, we can enable the custom stat group, confirm that the scope counters are registered correctly, and inspect the timing costs for each instrumented section of the Anim Graph.

Resulting:
![[Pasted image 20260301181028.png]]

#### Yea we name brand cause this is Adidas :D.

![[2026-03-01 18-18-26.mp4]]

![[Pasted image 20260301182237.png]]

![[2026-03-01 18-26-36.mp4]]

entries.title: Physia - Framework to solve Procedural Active Ragdolls
entries.body:
# Work in progress!

#### I'd get more into detail about the system in the future, if i find free time.
To cut it short its a System that articulates **Physical Bodies Procedurally** using Solvers to fill gaps where authored animations struggle or require extensive amounts of Animation Coverage.

<iframe width="560" height="315"  
src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/vGiD6DGbWx0"  
title="YouTube video"  
frameborder="0"  
allowfullscreen>  
</iframe>

---
Disclaimer: Containing mixed footage of old and new dev footage.

# Project Goals.

**Implemented.**
- Native API to articulate humanoid bodies.
- ImGui debugging to keep track and facilitate usage.
- Analytical Solvers to solve Bracing, Balancing, Foot-placement and many more.
- Custom IK Solver to control Limbs(Arms and Legs).
- From World to Ego rewrite, primarily to solve ML later.
- Exposed some of the functionality to BP_Graph.

**Forward Looking.**
- Create a system that is reliable, efficient and intuitive to use for designers.
- Expose more functionality to unreal's blueprint graph.
- Expose native functions and solvers to help with more complex tasks.

**Level 2.**
- Create a Machine Learning Pipeline to facilitate training of physical models.
- Supply Pre-trained Model's for step and balancing tasks, to provide out of the box, more grounded and natural results.

entries.title: Concept and Introduction
entries.body:
### Limitations of Traditional Look-At Solvers

Traditional look-at solvers usually offer limited control. 
Most simply use a look-at constraint to orient a bone towards a point of interest in the world. 
This works to a certain degree, but humans do more than that.

More complex solvers can introduce issues across poses. 
Forces may blend out in certain scenarios, which could easily break the overall pose. 
Solving look-at constraints additively on top of existing animation can cause further problems. 
For example, if the authored animation already has the character looking left, the head may overextend and overshoot the target for a short period before settling back.

Now, what can we do to solve this?

### I Googled, it’s fresh, **the first one**!

I present a novel approach to solving look-ats that introduces a **state machine system**, allowing for finer control across states such as gaits, stance, emotion and context. 

### Conveying Emotion Beyond Facial Expressions.

Facial expressions are not the only thing that define emotion, posture plays a key role as well. 
If I am angry, I may tilt my head down; similarly, I may look down when intimidated. 
Looking up can convey dominance, while leaning my head left or right adds nuance. 
These subtle movements support a character’s believability and help convey emotion beyond facial expressions

### Eyes don't lie!

Eyes were important to me too, and I focused on integrating solving for eyes as well, parametrizing features, as those can change how a character feels based on states like being drunk or under the influence of substances.

So, based on key observations made from assumptions splitting characteristics, I tried to expose full control over the feel of characters depending on the states described above.

### Solving Chains.

Per-bone controlled contribution to the authored pose further allows us to dial in and tweak the system.

To avoid expensive evaluation, we use a root-to-tip solve. 
I considered introducing forward-backward passes iterating a couple of times to distribute the contribution across the whole chain, but this was not necessary. 
The simple approach already gives great results, especially considering the state machine.

A tip-to-root solve would be slightly more computationally expensive, 
In fact, it could be problematic without a forward-backward solving pass, 
as the positioning of the chain may shift unpredictably.

### Constraints and Anatomical Correctness.

Similarly to creating constraints for a physically articulated body, parent-space constraints were crucial to keep the joints in natural poses and ensure the look-at solver did not produce anatomically incorrect orientations. 
Furthermore, the system is designed to allow these constraints to be modified at runtime.

### Mix And Mash.

By using look-at configurations that switch based on a state machine, 
the look-at node blends naturally, 
avoiding pops regardless of how complex the new configuration is. 
This approach allows designers to create situation-specific configurations and blend between them seamlessly using a state machine, either natively or through Unreal’s editor node graphs.

### Flexibility Across Characters.

Furthermore, it was important to ensure the system could handle complex characters and a variety of creatures, allowing the same solver to be repurposed without creating custom solutions for each archetype.

Imagine a Medusa with 50 snakes on her head, yep, works.

Rig conventions and transforms differ across rigs, which is why it is important to expose these settings explicitly rather than making assumptions.

### Outro.

I hope this gives you a general idea of the approach to take going forward if you want to create a similar/better system. 
I intentionally haven’t included code snippets or source code; 
my goal is to provoke thought and let you design the solution based on your own ideas.

Results here : [[L-A Slides]].

entries.title: Getting Started
entries.body:
To get started, we’ll likely want to **download it if you haven’t already**: [[Download]]

#### Okay, great, let’s start.  
Opening the Anim Graph, we would likely navigate to the **Procedural Anim Layer**.  
Right-clicking, we search for a node called: **PA_TK_LookAt**.  
This node appears :)
![[Screenshot 2026-03-01 153436.png]]

#### Now, at first it doesn’t look like much, but let’s check the **Details Panel**, shall we?
![[Pasted image 20260301154152.png]]

Let’s ignore the **Fallback sections**, since their sole purpose is **backwards compatibility** with older iterations.

- **Annotated first**: This is our **Look At Target Location**, which defines and sets the point in **world space** that we want the character to focus on.

- **Second**: Exposes the **Look At Config**, which holds all the necessary data to solve the look-at.

Here, we want to:

1. Click the **Bind** button and expose the pin.
2. Drag off the node and **promote it to a variable**.

Finally, **compile and save**!

#### Look At Config.

Lets Look at the Look at Config!
![[Pasted image 20260301155506.png]]

The first thing appearing is the **Bones** area, which holds a collection of **structurized bone configurations** for our affected bone chain, more on that later.

The second are the **Eyes**, same here, but solved differently.

Then we have our **Max Look At Angle in Degrees**, which is **per bone level**, always relative to the parent. 
Let’s set it to **90** for now.

**Look At Target Smooth Speed** uses **spherical interpolation smoothing**, which helps when the target changes focus, moving towards the target relative to the component, our character.

**Config Blend Speed** controls how quickly a newly blended config blends in, this is useful if we use a **state machine** otherwise can be ignored.

#### Look At Config.

##### Lets add a bone!
![[Pasted image 20260301160749.png]]

lets assign our first bone in the chain!:
![[Pasted image 20260301160945.png]]

Moving forward, we have our **local space axis conventions**.  
This means we need to check which axes our rig uses: the **forward axis** the one we want pointing in the direction towards the target, and the **up axis**, the one that points up basically :).  
Let’s open our rig and **validate which axes these are**.
![[Pasted image 20260301161514.png]]
Y Forward, X Up!

Okay:
![[Pasted image 20260301161813.png]]

Now we have the **Forward Axis Offset Rotation**, which we can tweak later **at runtime**!  
The purpose of this is simple: sometimes a bone doesn’t point exactly at the target. This offset lets us **adjust the vector** so the bone correctly aligns with where we want it to look.


#### STAY INSIDE!!!
![[Pasted image 20260301162352.png]]
These are the **limits we can set**, which control our **constraint space**.  
Relative to the parent, they define how much the joint can move using a **swing-twist solve**.  
We can **adjust these at runtime**, making it much easier to configure our Look-At configuration.

**Constraint Frame Rotation** allows us to **offset our constraint space**, similar to how we do it with the **Forward Axis Offset Rotation**.  
It’s important to **tweak this after setting the Forward Axis Offset**, so everything aligns correctly.

**Max Angular Speed (Deg)** is a **dead variable**, so it can be ignored!

**Look At Blend Weight** controls the **overall procedural contribution** to the pose.

And lastly, **Blend Damping Speed** controls **how quickly we orient toward the target**!

Let’s add all the other bones. The important part is to **verify the axis conventions**.  
To speed up the process, we can **duplicate the bone configurations multiple times** and switch the affected bones.  
The spine chain usually follows a similar convention, but **double-check everything with the asset** to verify the axes!

# Now let’s begin! This is our **baseline**!

![[Pasted image 20260301164404.png]]
We should have **something looking like this now**!

Remember, our **Target Location** is at **World 0,0,0**, unless you’ve already replaced it!  
We want to move to a location **close to it**.  
If that’s not possible, we can **drag a sphere in, copy its world location**, and set that value in our Anim Graph.

Spawning inside the world, our **character should already be looking at something**!
But that may not be exactly what we want, so we’re going to **dock our Anim Graph editor** to the **opposite side of our PIE viewport**.  
This way, we can **edit and visualize our constraints** in real time!

With the **struct open on one side** and the **PIE on the other**, we’re going to type in a command that lets us **visualize our constraints and edit them accordingly**:
``a.proc.lookat.debug 1``

![[Pasted image 20260301165751.png]]

Daniel may say! : Cool, very nice visualization!

After tweaking and configuring the config, we want to **save the adjusted values** and likely duplicate it to use as our **baseline**. Let’s rename it and call it **`LookAt_Configurator`**.

We’re able to duplicate it multiple times depending on how many states we want. The baseline could represent our **Idle/Standing**, while additional ones can be created per **gait** and **stance**.
If we plan to use a **state machine**, we should also create one called **`Runtime_LookAt_Config`**.
That may look something like what’s visualized here: [[Simple State Machine!]]

Now, considering all of this, our system could be used to solve **Aim Offsets** and **general Look-Ats**.  
I even tested some applications using a **flashlight to drive an arm chain**, it wasn’t designed for that, but hey, we’re allowed to play! You can see this in our [[L-A Slides]] preview.

Apart from that, it has also been tested for **directional blocking in combat situations** or **various movement scenarios during gaits**, which worked great and **expanded the range of motion** without requiring any additional animation authoring.  
I hope to be able to **reveal more soon**!
